sections.heading: Abstract
sections.text:
Low frequency piezoelectric P(VDF-TrFE) micro-cantilever vibration sensors have been developed for the first time with a novel MEMS process. Design and simulation of microcantilevers were carried out using COMSOL Multiphysics based on finite element method. Frequencies and device dimensions were determined based on simulation results. The design was implemented on $\langle 1 1 0 \rangle$ Si wafer using a specially developed bulk micromachining process. Micro-cantilevers were fabricated with $2 . 5 \mu \mathrm { { m } }$ thick P(VDF-TrFE) co-polymer film deposited by spin coating technique; electrodes for power output were formed by sequential thermal evaporation of Cr-Au thin films. The two critical process steps used for the suspension of P(VDF-TrFE) micro-cantilevers are: (1) bulk micromachining of silicon from the backside using anisotropic wet etchant TMAH to define the micro-cantilever suspension regions, and (2) $\mathrm { C H F } _ { 3 } / \mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ based plasma etching of $\mathrm { S i O } _ { 2 }$ from backside for the final release of P(VDF-TrFE) micro-cantilevers. These devices were operated in longitudinal mode with Cr-Au interdigitated electrodes on P(VDF-TrFE) micro-cantilevers for power extraction. The experimental results obtained with laser Doppler vibrometer for micro-cantilevers with $1 0 0 0 \ \mu \mathrm { { m } }$ length, $3 0 0 \ \mu \mathrm { { m } }$ width and $2 . 5 \ \mu \mathrm { m }$ thickness showed resonant frequency $4 7 7 . 0 3 \ : \mathrm { H z }$ and power output $1 8 7 . 4 \ \mathrm { p W }$ for tip displacement $3 1 2 . 5 \ \mu \mathrm { m }$ which are closely in agreement with the simulated values 453.65 $\mathrm { H z }$ and $1 8 9 ~ \mathrm { p W }$ for tip displacement $3 1 0 ~ \mu \mathrm { m }$ , respectively. The volume power density of this P(VDF-TrFE) unimorph micro-cantilever is $2 4 9 . 9 \dot { 2 } \ \mathrm { n W } \mathrm { m m } ^ { - 3 }$ , which is found to be better compared with other polymer piezoelectric cantilevers.

Keywords: micro-electromechanical systems (MEMS), piezoelectric, P(VDF-TrFE) co-polymer, micro-cantilevers, vibration sensors, energy harvesters

sections.heading: 1. Introduction
sections.text:
Over the past several years, micro-electromechanical systems (MEMS) based devices have found applications in a variety of technologies which include inertial navigation systems [1], medical devices [2], wireless communication [3], pressure sensors [4], accelerometers [5] and others. For applications such as pressure sensors, accelerometers etc piezoelectric materials are essential. Among the most common piezoelectric materials, inorganic piezoelectric materials such as lead zirconium titanate (PZT) [6] and organic/polymer piezoelectric materials like Polyvinylidene fluoride (PVDF)

and its co-polymers are important. Although the piezoelectric ceramic materials have found applications in MEMS devices [7–9], their use is limited in low frequency applications [10–13] due to their high $k$ factor (spring constant) which results in higher natural frequencies. On the other hand, there has been increasing interest in piezoelectric polymer materials for low frequency applications such as vibration sensors, energy harvesters etc due to their soft and flexible nature resulting in lower natural frequencies. Further, their lower electromechanical coupling factors, low dielectric and good piezoelectric properties are an added advantage.

Among the piezoelectric polymers, PVDF is the most commonly used polymer due to its high flexibility, low cost and good piezoelectric properties [4, 5, 14–17]. Hence, PVDF has been used in various applications, which include pressure sensors [4], accelerometers [5], tactile sensors [15], ultrasonic transducers [16] and energy harvesters [17]. However, PVDF requires a mechanical stretching (poling) to change from nonpolar $\alpha$ -phase to dipolar $\beta$ -phase which is essential for piezoelectricity. Hence, this is a disadvantage. More serious however, is the fact that polymers such as PVDF is incompatible with MEMS processing which involves strong chemicals, plasma processing etc. Hence, the use of PVDF as a piezoelectric material is very limited in MEMS devices such as micro-cantilevers, micro-cantilever beams and similar devices for the development of low frequency vibration sensors.

The co-polymer Poly (vinylidine fluoride-trifluoroethylene) P(VDF-TrFE) crystallizes with $1 3 0 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ anneal into dipolar $\beta$ -phase without any mechanical stretching [18]. Further, P(VDF-TrFE) has better piezoelectric properties than PVDF [19]. Hence, P(VDF-TrFE) is a promising piezoelectric co-polymer for the development of vibration sensors. However, integration of the co-polymer micro-cantilever fabrication process with standard MEMS device processing involving strong chemicals or etchants has been a serious challenge; understandably therefore, there has been little success so far in the fabrication of P(VDF-TrFE) micro-cantilevers using Si MEMS technology.

This work demonstrates first successful fabrication of unimorph $d _ { 3 3 }$ mode P(VDF-TrFE) micro-cantilevers using a novel Si bulk micromachining process. The micro-cantilevers consist of an active piezoelectric P(VDF-TrFE) layer with $\mathrm { C r } -$ Au interdigitated electrodes (IDE). The dimensions of the unimorph micro-cantilevers were optimized using finite element analysis with COMSOL Multiphysics simulation software. The details of design, simulation, fabrication and measurement results are presented here.

Figure 1 shows a schematic of a piezoelectric micro-cantilever which consists of an active P(VDF-TrFE) co-polymer as a piezoelectric layer. The figure also shows the IDE pattern of $\mathrm { C r - A u }$ layer for sensing the electrical power from the device. With low frequency applications in mind we have optimised microcantilever device dimensions with simulation software COMSOL Multiphysics.

The resonant frequency of a micro-cantilever is one of the most important design parameters because each microcantilever has the maximum power output when the vibration frequency matches with the resonant frequency of the piezoelectric micro-cantilever and that power output will be reduced drastically when the vibration frequency deviates from the resonant frequency of the device. The resonant frequency of a micro-cantilever depends on its dimensions and the material constants. In addition, cantilevers have several modes of vibrations, with different resonant frequencies. The first mode of vibration has the lowest resonant frequency with maximum displacement and hence, maximum power output. The resonant frequency of a micro-cantilever is given by the following expression:

$$
f _ { \mathrm { n } } = \frac { k } { 2 \pi L ^ { 2 } } \sqrt { \frac { I } { m } } ,
$$

where $f _ { \mathrm { n } }$ corresponds to $\mathrm { n } ^ { \mathrm { t h } }$ mode resonant frequency, $k$ is the spring constant of the micro-cantilever, $I$ is the bending modulus, $L$ is the length of the micro-cantilever and $m$ is the mass/unit area which can be calculated by thickness, length, width and density of the micro-cantilever [20].

Even though there are many piezoelectric vibration modes, $d _ { 3 1 }$ and $d _ { 3 3 }$ modes are the most commonly used modes in piezoelectric devices [21, 22]. They are distinguished by whether the electric field direction is perpendicular to the input strain direction $\left( d _ { 3 1 } \right.$ mode) or parallel to it $\ b { d _ { 3 3 } }$ mode). sections.heading: 2. Design and simulation
sections.text:
A micro-cantilever is a device free at one end and anchored at the other end. Hence, it generates significantly high strains in response to relatively low stress forces. The resonant frequency of micro-cantilever depends on its dimensions and spring constant of the material used. Therefore, by choosing appropriate device dimensions and using materials with low $$ \begin{array} { c } { { x _ { 3 } = d _ { 3 i } E _ { i } , } } \\ { { { } } } \\ { { V _ { 3 i } = \sigma _ { x x } g _ { 3 i } L _ { i } , } } \end{array} $$ where $d _ { 3 i }$ and $g _ { 3 i }$ are piezoelectric constants and $L _ { i }$ represents distance between electrodes [23]. For power extraction, the $d _ { 3 1 }$ mode requires separate top and bottom electrodes, whereas the $d _ { 3 3 }$ mode eliminates need for bottom electrode with an IDE pattern on top surface. The $d _ { 3 3 }$ mode design gives much higher open-circuit voltage than the $d _ { 3 1 }$ mode at similar micro-cantilever dimensions and also the use of $d _ { 3 3 }$ mode reduces the complexity of fabrication, since only one level of electrode pattern is required [24]. The P(VDF-TrFE) micro-cantilevers were designed for unimorph $d _ { 3 3 }$ mode and its mechanical and electrical responses were simulated with COMSOL Multiphysics simulation software. Using the parameters in table 2 which contain the default material properties in COMSOL material library as well as the values obtained from the experiment, 3D-finite element method based partial differential equation solver was used to simulate micro-cantilevers. The resonant frequency, voltage and power output of the micro-cantilevers were simulated by applying boundary conditions such as fixed end, applied vibration and damping. The device dimensions were designed and frequencies were obtained through simulation using equation (1). Simulations were carried out for P(VDF-TrFE) micro-cantilevers with thickness $2 . 5 \ \mu \mathrm { m }$ , width in the range 100 to $3 0 0 \ \mu \mathrm { { m } }$ and length in the range $2 0 0 { \mathrm { - } } 1 0 0 0 \ \mu \mathrm { m }$ . Shown in figures 2(a) and (b) are the simulation results of a micro-cantilever with width $3 0 0 \ \mu \mathrm { { m } }$ and length $1 0 0 0 \mu \mathrm { m }$ with an optimal load of $4 5 \mathrm { { M }Omega }$ . sections.heading: 3. Device fabrication
sections.text: The simulated MEMS based P(VDF-TrFE) micro-cantilevers were fabricated using a novel silicon bulk micromachining process. Three photo masks were used in this fabrication process as shown in the schematics in figure 3. A p-type $\langle 1 1 0 \rangle$ oriented silicon wafer $5 0 ~ \mathrm { ~ m m }$ diameter, $3 0 0 ~ \mu \mathrm { { m } }$ thickness was wet oxidised to obtain $1 \mu \mathrm m$ thick silicon dioxide $\mathrm { ( S i O } _ { 2 } )$ layer on both sides of the wafer. The $\mathrm { S i O } _ { 2 }$ layer on the backside of the wafer was patterned through standard photolithography process using first level mask to obtain a backside rectangular window which defines the suspension regions of P(VDF-TrFE) micro-cantilever. Then access to the backside silicon was obtained by etching the patterned $\mathrm { S i O } _ { 2 }$ using 5:1 buffered oxide etch. The exposed Si was then etched completely using an alkaline solution $2 5 \mathrm { \ u t } \%$ tetramethylammonium hydroxide (TMAH). $\mathrm { S i O } _ { 2 }$ layer on the front side acts as an etch-stop layer resulting in thin diaphragm on the front side which serves as an initial support for P(VDF-TrFE) micro-cantilever during this bulk micromachining process. The piezoelectric P(VDF-TrFE) film layer was then deposited on front side of the wafer using spin coating technique. Solutions used for P(VDF-TrFE) film was prepared using N, N-dimethylacetamide and P(VDF-TrFE) powder with $7 0 / 3 0$ molar ratio. In order to obtain the required thickness of P(VDF-TrFE) co-polymer film, $2 . 5 \ \mu \mathrm { { m } }$ (measured by DektakXT Profilometer), spin coating was performed in two steps: first, the wafer was spun at $3 0 0 \mathrm { r p m }$ for $1 0 \mathrm s$ , followed by a spin at $1 0 0 0 \mathrm { r p m }$ for $3 0 \mathrm { s }$ ; followed by 15 min of solvent evaporation at $1 2 0 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ and anneal at $1 3 0 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ for $^ { 3 \mathrm { ~ h ~ } }$ to improve the crystallinity and introduce the $\beta$ phase of the co-polymer film. After annealing of the wafer, a $\mathrm { C r - A u }$ layer $\mathrm { \bf C r - } 1 0 \ \mathrm { n m }$ and Au- $1 4 0 ~ \mathrm { n m }$ ) was deposited sequentially by thermal evaporation. A second level masking is then carried out to define the micro-cantilever regions by using the Cr-Au layer as a mask. For this the exposed $\mathrm { C r - A u }$ layers were etched sequentially using Au and $\mathrm { C r }$ etchants. Wet etchants were used to etch gold (mixture of KI, $\mathrm { I } _ { 2 }$ and Deionized (DI) water) and chromium (mixture of $\mathrm { ( N H _ { 4 } ) _ { 2 } C e }$ $\left( \mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } \right)$ , $\mathrm { H C l O _ { 4 } }$ and DI water) with minimum over-etching to minimize swelling of the P(VDF-TrFE) layer. The morphology of P(VDF-TrFE) film under the Cr-Au layers remained unchanged during the patterning process (shown in figure 5(a)). To reduce the effect of swelling and degradation of P(VDF-TrFE) film in wet chemicals, $\mathrm { C H F } _ { 3 } / \mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ based plasma etching technique was used to define the P(VDF-TrFE) micro-cantilevers. The thin layer of Cr-Au serves as a mask for the P(VDF-TrFE) micro-cantilevers during plasma etching. The required IDE structure of Cr-Au film was then obtained by patterning and etching of gold and chromium sequentially using a third level mask. Finally, the P(VDF-TrFE) micro-cantilevers were released by etching the thin diaphragm of $\mathrm { S i O } _ { 2 }$ underneath the micro-cantilevers. This critical etching process was carried out in $\mathrm { C H F } _ { 3 } / \mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ based plasma system optimized for etching $\mathrm { S i O } _ { 2 }$ with an etch rate of $2 0 \mathrm { n m } \mathrm { m i n } ^ { - 1 }$ . The P(VDF-TrFE) micro-cantilevers fabricated had lengths ranging from 200 to $1 0 0 0 \mu \mathrm { m }$ and widths ranging from 100 to $3 0 0 \ \mu \mathrm { { m } }$ with thickness $2 . 5 \ \mu \mathrm { m }$ in all cases.

sections.heading: 4.2. Device measurements
sections.text:
The resonant frequency, tip displacement, voltage and power output of micro-cantilevers were measured using dynamic signal analyzer (DSA) and Polytec MSA-500 Micro-system laser Doppler vibrometer (LDV). In this system, the microcantilever is excited by an electromagnetic shaker controlled by a function generator which sweeps the frequency through a voltage amplifier. An uni-axis piezoelectric accelerometer, which is fixed on the top of the device holder, is used for measurement of the micro-cantilever excitation. Further, the laser beam from the LDV is directed on the micro-cantilever and the vibration amplitudes are measured from Doppler shift of the reflected laser beam. A differential laser interferometer is used to measure the Doppler shift which gives the tip displacement of the micro-cantilever. A resistive load is connected to the micro-cantilever in order to measure the voltage, current and power output of the micro-cantilever under excitation. The DSA displays the variation of displacement, voltage and power output with frequency. Measurements were carried out on P(VDF-TrFE) microcantilevers using LDV and variation of tip displacement, voltage and power output were extracted as a function of frequency. Figure 6(a) shows the tip displacement of a typical device, $1 0 0 0 \ \mu \mathrm { { m } }$ length, $3 0 0 \ \mu \mathrm { { m } }$ width and $2 . 5 \ \mu \mathrm { m }$ thickness as a function of frequency. The measured tip displacement is $3 1 2 . 5 \ \mu \mathrm { m }$ at the resonant frequency of $4 7 7 . 0 3 ~ \mathrm { H z }$ . This is nearly in agreement with the simulated results giving tip displacement $3 1 0 ~ \mu \mathrm { { m } }$ at the resonant frequency $4 5 3 . 6 5 ~ \mathrm { H z }$ . Simulated power output of the micro-cantilever, $1 8 9 \mathrm { p W }$ also matches with the experimentally measured value of $1 8 7 . 4 \mathrm { p W }$ at an optimal load of $4 5 \mathbf { M } \Omega$ (shown in figure 6(b)). Further, the experimentally obtained power output and also volume power densities are compared with those reported in the literature for other piezoelectric cantilevers. Table 4 shows comparison of power output and resonant frequency obtained in this work with other piezoelectric cantilevers published in the literature. The important point to note here is that while the absolute power is lower here since the cantilevers are in the micro-domain, this novel fabrication process can indeed be extended to fabricate macro-cantilevers as well with higher power outputs. Another advantage of this process is that it is possible to fabricate or develop a series of micro/macro cantilevers on the same silicon chip to tailor the frequency/ power range as desired. ![](images/4a7bbefa1680fc2a8e7ffc9a2024a9d019862703fdec016c73d645ae0c75f848.jpg) Figure 6. sections.heading: 5. Conclusion
sections.text:
In conclusion, we have presented the design, simulation, fabrication and performance characterization of MEMS based piezoelectric low frequency P(VDF-TrFE) micro-cantilevers.

A novel Si bulk micromachining process has been developed to successfully fabricate P(VDF-TrFE) micro-cantilevers for the first time. Using the default material properties available in COMSOL Multiphysics library, as well as experimentally obtained value of $d _ { 3 3 }$ , simulations were carried out for P(VDF-TrFE) micro-cantilevers with thickness $2 . 5 \quad \mu \mathrm { m } .$ widths in the range 100 to $3 0 0 \ \mu \mathrm { { m } }$ and lengths in the range $2 0 0 { \mathrm { - } } 1 0 0 0 \ \mu \mathrm { m }$ . The P(VDF-TrFE) micro-cantilevers fabricated had lengths ranging from 200 to $1 0 0 0 \ \mu \mathrm { { m } }$ and widths ranging from 100 to $3 0 0 \ \mu \mathrm { { m } }$ with thickness $2 . 5 \ \mu \mathrm { { m } }$ in all cases. Micro-cantilevers were characterised using LDV. The results obtained for the longest device $1 0 0 0 \ \mu \mathrm { { m } }$ length with width $3 0 0 \ \mu \mathrm { { m } }$ and thickness $2 . 5 \ \mu \mathrm { m }$ showed resonance frequency $4 7 7 . 0 3 \ \mathrm { H z }$ , tip displacement $3 1 2 . 5 \ \mu \mathrm { m }$ and power output $1 8 7 . 4 \mathrm { \ p W }$ . These are nearly in agreement with the simulated values $4 5 3 . 6 5 ~ \mathrm { H z }$ , $3 1 0 ~ \mu \mathrm { m }$ and $1 8 9 \ \mathrm { p W }$ , respectively. The experimentally obtained power output and also volume power densities are compared with those reported in the literature for other piezoelectric cantilevers and found to be better than other polymer piezoelectric cantilevers. Further, these results show that this novel process has the potential for the development of P(VDF-TrFE) micro/macro-cantilevers and their arrays on a single silicon chip for low frequency vibration sensor/energy harvester device applications.
